title: Saccaka's boast
hook: a famous debater boasts he will shake the Buddha, and sweats instead

segments.voice: Yesterday: gopalaka, and your line, know your herd. Which of the eleven small skills did you try on purpose? Day four hundred thirty.

In the city of Vesali there lives a debater named Saccaka, and he is very good. He says so himself. He tells crowds there is no teacher alive who wouldn't shake and tremble if he debated them. Even a post, he says, would shake if he argued with it, never mind a human being. Then he hears what the Buddha teaches, and he announces he'll go and drag him around like a man dragging a sheep by its fleece. Five hundred people come to watch. Today: Saccaka's boast.
screen: `A DEBATER IN VESALI.` → `EVEN A POST WOULD SHAKE.` → `FIVE HUNDRED COME TO WATCH.`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the shorter discourse to Saccaka. Saccaka opens. He says the body is my self, feeling is my self, perception, mental formations, consciousness: all of these are my self. The Buddha doesn't argue back at once. He asks a question. A king rules his country. Can he have someone executed, fined or banished? Of course, says Saccaka. Then you say the body is your self. Can you command it: let my body be like this, don't let it be like that? Saccaka goes silent. The Buddha asks again. Silence again. The text adds a dramatic touch: a spirit named Vajirapani hovers above with a thunderbolt, and only Saccaka and the Buddha can see him. The Buddha asks a third time, and Saccaka answers: no. I can't command it. Then the same for feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. If it can't be commanded, and it changes, and it brings pain when it changes, is it fit to call it mine, I, my self? No. At the end, sweat pours from Saccaka's forehead, soaks through his robe and drips to the ground. The Buddha notes, gently, that there's no sweat on his own body. And one of the crowd says Saccaka looks like a crab with its legs broken, unable to crawl back into its pond. Here's the turn: Saccaka isn't a villain. He invites the Buddha and the monks to a meal the next day, and later he comes back for another talk, which we hear tomorrow. Certainty that has never been tested can sweat when it finally is.
screen: `THE BODY IS MY SELF, SAYS SACCAKA` · `A KING RULES; CAN YOU RULE YOUR BODY?` · `SILENCE, THEN NO` · `SWEAT ON HIS ROBE, NONE ON THE BUDDHA` · then, large: `THE SWEAT OF CERTAINTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one boast pass. Sit, and try the Buddha's question on yourself. Tell your body: don't let this knee ache, don't let my mind wander. Then watch what happens over the next minute. Notice the body and mind doing what they do, whether you command them or not. No sweat required. If a little thought of 'I'm good at this' shows up, let it pass too, like Saccaka's crowd going home. The bell holds the time.
Saccaka's boast. The debater who said even a post would shake before him, and ended up sweating, then coming back for more. Today's word.
Your line: the sweat of certainty. Today, when you feel very sure in an argument, ask yourself one honest question before you answer. Day four hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 35's question, whether we can command the body and mind to be as we wish, as a classic way into the teaching of not-self (anatta) and the five aggregates.

myth: the Buddha won by out-arguing Saccaka point by point
he asked a question: can you command your body to be as you wish? Saccaka's silence did the rest.
Saccaka sweated through his robe while the Buddha didn't sweat
the text says Saccaka's sweat dripped to the ground, and the Buddha's body had none.
Saccaka left angry and never came back
he invited the Buddha to a meal, and returned for another conversation in MN 36.

fork.setup: you're Saccaka. the Buddha asks: can you command your body, 'let it be like this, not like that'? five hundred people are watching. what do you do?
options: change the subject to the weather.
fork.reveal: Saccaka stays silent twice. asked a third time, he admits: no. then the sweat starts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about the Buddha winning a debate.
what it means: what changes, can't be commanded and brings pain isn't fit to be called 'mine, I, my self'.

what a scholar hears: Saccaka is called a son of the Niganthas (the Jain tradition) and an Aggivessana by clan, and his question-and-answer here closely echoes the discourse on the characteristic of not-self (SN 22.59), which tradition counts as the Buddha's second sermon.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 35, Culasaccaka Sutta (the shorter discourse to Saccaka)
Samyutta Nikaya 22.59, Anattalakkhana Sutta (the characteristic of not-self)

notes: MN 35 paraphrased: Saccaka's boast (even an insentient post would shake), the 'sheep by the fleece' image, the king simile, Vajirapani with the thunderbolt, the sweat, Dummukha's crab simile, the meal invitation. Confirm each detail. The crowd size (five hundred Licchavis) also to confirm.
Vajirapani is described as a spirit (yakkha); the script says 'a spirit' to keep it plain.
Saccaka's family background (son of Nigantha parents) is stated neutrally; Jain sources do not record this debate.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Vajirapani is seen by both Saccaka and the Buddha in MN 35 (script had 'only Saccaka'); 'second discourse' for SN 22.59 now attributed to tradition; softened 'often sweats'.
